newsitem.title: CHINA: Competition hits prices of Chinese motorcycles.
newsitem.headline: Competition hits prices of Chinese motorcycles.

text.p: Excess production and fierce competition in China's motorcycle market has driven prices down and threatens to push smaller manufacturers into bankruptcy, industry officials said on Friday.
Since April, motorcycle prices in China have fallen by about 10 percent due to heavy competition and a reduction that month of the tariff on imported models to 70 percent from 120 percent, they said.

The tariff cut probably had only a small impact because imported models are too expensive for most Chinese consumers, said an official of Jinan Qinqi Motorcycles Co Ltd, one of China's biggest motorcycle manufacturers.
"But price falls are inevitable because there are too many producers and output is far beyond demand," he said.
In the first half of 1996, China produced 4.28 million motorcycles but sold only 3.8 million, official figures show. In 1995, China produced 7.8 million but sold 6.1 million.
Over the past five years, China has produced 20 million motorcycles, with output growing 52 percent annually, the Shanghai Wen Hui Bao newspaper said on Thursday.

"China has become the world's biggest motorcycle market since 1993, with domestic demand rising sharply with development of its economy," said an official of China Jialing Industrial Group Co Ltd, another major manufacturer.
"But the market is saturated now, with an increasing number of producers and restrictions on the use of motorcycles in most cities," she said.

In most cities, getting a licence to operate a motorcycle costs as much as the motorcycle itself because local governments -- concerned with worsening traffic congestion and air pollution -- try to discourage motorcycle purchases.
The results of the price war are shrinking profit margins for manufacturers, with margins falling to as low as 30-40 yuan ($3.6-4.8) per model, the official from Jinan Qinqi Motor said.
"No producer wants to go out of business and everyone tries their best to sell more of their products, with little concern for current profits," he said.

There are 300 producers in China but only 10 make more than 100,000 units a year and only four make more than 500,000, she said. The government wants 8-12 big producers by 2000 and three or four by 2010, the Jialing official said, adding that a restructuring of the industry was inevitable.

"Most small competitors will disappear after the price war and the market is likely to be dominated by several giants," she said. "The same story has happened in China's colour television and microwave oven markets this year."
Those markets also suffer from over-production.
China's biggest colour television producer, Sichuan Changhong Electric Appliances Co Ltd, cut prices by between eight and 18 percent in March, forcing other major domestic producers to follow suit.

The same thing happened in August, when Galanz, one of China's biggest manufacturers of microwave ovens, cut prices of its two major models by 40 percent in order to push small producers out of a crowded market.
